utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration. You've already made the declaration. Well, then you remain subject to it. Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I think it is my turn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Your turn.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Good morning, Dr. Tabeau. How are you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Good morning. Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: My name is Jason Alarid and I represent Milan Lukic. I just want to ask a few questions. I don't think this will take too long. With regards to your analysis just to kind of have a rehash as we're coming back a couple days later, the first set of data you used was of course the 1991 census?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And the second set of data you used was voter registration?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, had you done any long-standing demographic model that would take into consideration earlier censuses, quite possibly?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Not for this study but there is a table in the report in which I give numbers of the population in Visegrad since the 1948 census.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And is that broken down by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, it isn't. These are overall totals.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. What was the population growth over the model period?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: The population growth in terms of how much population increase?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yeah. I mean, were you able to --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please observe a pause. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Birth rates, things like that.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: I didn't study the population growth.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And I'm sorry, I need to turn on my microphone. Or my ear piece, rather. And so you couldn't tell just from looking at the data what was just people having children, of course, within the community versus people actually emigrating or moving and populating the area?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, this is not what we did in this study. We didn't study demographic trends, in fertility, in mortality, in migration. We observed the population of Visegrad on two moments of time, at the outbreak of the conflict 1991 census data and post-conflict population in the voters registration.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in the post-conflict information, were there any other data sets other than voter registration to compare against?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, except there was a small data set from the UNHCR that we used to -- for contextual purposes, and this data was on internally displaced persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And you didn't -- you didn't necessarily do any verification work for the Red Cross list, did you?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, we have done a lot of work on the Red Cross data, but tell me exactly what you mean with the verification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Meaning just investigative work to make sure that there's not any errors in the list that may have slipped through the cracks from the Red Cross perspective.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, this is what we've been always doing with every source and we checked the ICRC data for deficiencies, for incompleteness, for misreporting, but at the same time we cross-referenced this data with other sources in this project but also in other projects. For instance, in Srebrenica projects we cross-referenced the ICRC data with a DNA identification records, that is part of exhumation records, and ended with actually very good overlap of the DNA identifications with ICRC missing data.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, other than taking the list that was provided by the Prosecution and comparing it against -- and I'd say it's a list of Pionirska Street names and comparing it against the Red Cross database, did you do anything else to verify for the Visegrad area?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: You mean with other sources. We did compare the ICRC data -- well, records starting with the records from Pionirska Street. We used the ICRC data for cross-referencing. We used data from Bosnian book of death. We used ICMP records of the identified persons. We used BCMP that is the Bosnia commission for tracing missing persons. So we have done -- we used the RS mortality database to cross-reference these records. A lot of comparisons actually had been done with respect to the victim lists, including Pionirska records.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, did you cleanse the census?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, cleanse, what you mean by cleansing?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, what -- what efforts did you take to cleanse the 1991 census, to verify the accuracy of the census?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Or do you know if it was done?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: I know a lot of work has been done with the census data back in Bosnia and Herzegovina and also in my unit. Our focus was the spelling mistakes in the names, because we needed the names for matching with other sources, and we have done a lot of work to clean the names from mistakes, to end with good names that would be good overlapping with other sources. We of course studied JMBG and we studied date of birth. We wanted to know how much information is missing. Well, I believe a lot of work has been done here, and also a lot of work has been done in Bosnia, although I must say one part of the census, agricultural part, which we didn't use, wasn't actually cleansed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the transcript, Mr. Alarid, may I draw your attention that there is the list of adjudicated facts and the census is part of the facts that we accepted as adjudicated facts, and maybe this may allow you to focus your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: That would, Your Honour, thank you, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, did you discover if Bosnia post-war post 1997 has undertaken a census in the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: The 1991 census actually was the last one undertaken in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What was the -- in the United States it's every ten years. What was the pattern in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, until 1991 it was every ten years. Since 1991 we haven't had a census in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. Did you account for any kind of migration? I know that the Serbian population went up slightly between the two data sets, from 1991 to 1997. Did you account whether this was birth rate or actually migration, new people moving into the community?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, first of all Serbian population you mean the population of Republika Srpska or --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Of Visegrad, Visegrad?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Oh Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Of Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: The Serbs in Visegrad, Bosnian Serbs in Visegrad, well, how do you know the actual size of the population after the conflict in Visegrad --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: -- and any other municipality as well? So there was no census. We had the voters registration, which is a sample of the post-war population, a big sample, but it is not that. It is the size that you can conclude from this sample.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, and I guess because -- were your numbers in Visegrad in the 1997 voter registration sample, was that strictly people that had registered to vote?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: That is what -- what it was, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: So you don't have any accounting for their children who may not be of voting age?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: No. The children below age of 18 are not in the sample.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And anyone between 18 and 80 that doesn't want to register, you don't account for them?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: These people who didn't want to register or they couldn't register are not there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And in somewhat of a patriarchal society, you may not have women represented fairly in the census?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Not the census. I'm sorry, voter registration.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: I would be surprised if it was the case in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, and just a standpoint it wouldn't be uncommon for one spouse to register to vote and another spouse maybe not to register to vote?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, but I saw cases where one the same JMBG was used for the spouses, the wife and the husband.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, and understood, they might go as a couple to register but also were you able to verify marital status from voter registration?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Why would I be interested in marital status?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Only to compare and contrast the names, seeing if his wife is in fact registered?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, actually our interest was just to see changes in the place of residence of people. This was the crucial question of the study. So we didn't look at other aspects of the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, you can assume that there was some Muslim reintegration into the population. People did come home.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: What -- reintegration. When? What do you mean by integration?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, I mean --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please observe a pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You have to observe a pause between question and answer, both counsel and witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: What I mean by integration is or reintegration is it's possible some people did move back and simply didn't register to vote?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: First of all, I don't think there were many returns of minority groups on the first place Muslims being the minority group after the conflict ended in December 1995 until the elections, 1997, 1998. Well, this is one thing. Second thing, if they returned, actually, and physically lived in Visegrad, why wouldn't they register to vote and vote actually?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, because maybe they're scared.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't get this point, to be honest, because you know first of all you even didn't have to be there physically in Visegrad to vote for Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, if you move back and someone can go to a county building and check your ethnicity and your address from voter registration, that might be a fear factor for someone to reregister to vote?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: But they didn't have to register in Visegrad to vote for Visegrad. They could have done this from Sarajevo, from abroad, from anyplace. They could have registered anywhere and still vote for Visegrad. If you were so afraid to register, you could have gone to another place and register and then you would escape the attention that you voted actually for this municipality and your party?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: So I see no point in this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, because they were disenfranchised people. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: The conflict in and of itself disenfranchised them?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: I believe that the registration rate and participation rate in the elections of 1997 and 1998 was relatively high, so I can -- I even give a -- I gave an estimate of this in the report, and I have it here in the PowerPoint presentation. So we are speaking of a really big participation in these elections. So the sample of voters that we used in our analysis is without any doubt a big sample, solid data, absolutely more than good enough to estimate the ethnic composition, not the size of the population but most certainly the ethnic composition in the Visegrad in the post-conflict area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, if you -- if you register to vote in Sarajevo, you can vote for the local Visegrad election in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: If you registered, but if you can prove that you are eligible to vote you could register in Sarajevo and vote for Visegrad.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. That would be very inconvenient, though, wouldn't you say if you lived in Visegrad and you're poor?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: I wouldn't go into this discussion, because this is not any part of my report. So I gave you numbers. I gave you sample size. I gave you a good description of the voters registration, how it was done, who did it. I can tell you more about it, but I wouldn't like to go into these kind of things, how convenient or inconvenient it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm just -- I'm just exploring the possibilities that the Muslim side of that analysis from a voter registration standpoint could have some potential shortcomings, some unreported peoples that you just wouldn't be able to take into account. Not your fault but just the limitation of the data set.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: I wouldn't think so. I have never heard of ethnic differences in the registration rate for these elections. What I'm trying to say, I am absolutely unaware of the fact that one ethnic group in a given territory, in a given region, would register for the elections less than other ethnic groups. I -- I -- I have read several reports by the OSCE related to these elections, some annual reports, and I have never seen any comment of this kind in these reports. So I wouldn't believe there is an ethnic inequality in the registration rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, but -- but in fact the Visegrad Muslim -- oh, I'm sorry. But in fact the Visegrad Muslim population was identified based on ethnicity and then ultimately persecuted to a certain degree based on their ethnicity. So that's why I'm saying maybe they would have a real disincentive to reregister in the area for two reasons. One is simple fear that they could be reidentified by a similar means at some future conflict because they can't as a person eliminate that this wouldn't happen again, and also recognising what maybe you saw, which is a larger Serb population is now there so not registering from a well, my vote doesn't count, anyway, what deference am I going to make in this population because we are too few to gain seats. So there's two -- I believe two reasons that someone just, I'm not going to register here. Would that be plausible reasons?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm not with you on this. I think that I showed in my report that the Muslim population that was originally initially, the disparate in the population census that we identified in the voters registers, moved out from the municipality. I would take you now -- I will take you now to one of the tables in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Which table, ma'am?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Is it in your PowerPoint as well or just in the report?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, I prefer to go to the report. This is table 3B on page 13, English version.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: If it can assist its's marked for identification as Exhibit P118, 118.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: P118. Page 13. If the court assistant would bring that so we all can see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Page 13, table 3B. This table is composed of two parts. The upper panel are the absolute numbers, and the lower panel are percentages. So if you look at the Muslims in the first panel, there was an overall total of 6.799 individuals who initially were reported in the 1991 census data as part of the 1991 population, and this number we were able to identify in the voters registers. This is a big sample. Believe me, statistically speaking I'm very happy with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I know. I took statistics in college. I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: I'm happy we agree, so if we look at the distribution of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That's the problem, Mr. Alarid.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: That seems to be the problem. You took it in college.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So you want to show off your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, you know, Your Honour, sometimes I don't know what's relevant in the end of this thing so I'm trying to anticipate. I'm a little confused why we're dealing with so much statistics in an eyewitness case, but the Prosecution brings it, and so I feel like I need to address any inaccuracies if there can be, or limitations, but I agree. I'm very short after this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. I think you can move on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Shall I continue with this table?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Yes, sure, explain the table?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: So in the row for Muslims we see a distribution of the Muslim population who initially was reported in the census and later found in the voters register by place of post-conflict residence. So one person, exactly one person stayed in Visegrad municipality. This is the first column titled "This municipality." The next two columns, "Other municipalities" and "Out of country" show us the numbers from the sample of Muslims who moved out from Visegrad. So it is the overall number of 6.798 persons. Just the overall total minus one who are reported in other places, not in Visegrad anymore. So it is not a question of underregistration, of not being there in the sample. They are there. They are in big numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: In other places?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: In other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: So this is how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Just a couple more questions. Did you account for the fact that there might have been a nonregistered-to-vote population before that date, just from the rural and agrarian side of the population?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't get the question now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Well, I mean were there voter registrations in 1991?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: The voters elections in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: The voter registration.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't understand the question, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you look at voter registration in 1991?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. And I guess comparing the people that were registered to vote, what percentage of the population because that's important in any population is what percentage of the adult voting population that can vote actually registered because there is of course a section of the population that chooses not to.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, I now take you to my PowerPoint presentation, please, and to page -- which page. I'm looking for the right page. Right. To page 15, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: If it would assist I can give a copy for the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So what we've been discussing today is actually summarised on page 15 in my PowerPoint presentation. I never claimed that the sample of voters is complete covering the entire population. The children are there. The unregistered voters are there. On the contrary, I on this sheet explicitly mention what is missing in the voters. One of the issues I discuss is the unregistered voters. This is the last paragraph. So you read there the exact number is unknown of those who are unregistered, but following the OSCE we estimate that about 12 per cent of the population, 1997, 1998, population of eligible voters did not register. The 12 per cent of eligible voters. Now, the 12 per cent of eligible voters can be easily obtained using the data from this report, because in one of the tables in the report I give the overall total of eligible voters, which is 17.800 approximately. So 12 per cent of this total gives you the 2.146. That would be the unregistered voters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Now, this -- I'm not sure the answer to this question, but did you do a similar analysis for the Serb Muslim population on the other side of the Dayton line?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Of the Dayton line. Well, you don't believe that the Muslims who moved out from Visegrad stayed in the RS area. I believe there is a table in the report that shows again where they went to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: No. That's not really the question. Did you -- the country was split in half?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And so my point is did you do an analysis for the other side of the country?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. In several reports we analysed areas at both sites of the Dayton line in both political entities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Did you -- were you able to show areas where the Serbian population had gone down in a particular area and the Muslim population of course had gone up probably from this side?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. It is a two-way process. So the Muslim population was moving out from the territories controlled by the RS authority, and the Serbian population was moving out from the territories controlled by the Bosnian government. So that was -- I never said it was a one-way process. So Muslims moved out from Visegrad and Serbs moved out from other territories.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay. Did you do any --

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Have new newcomers in Visegrad, Serbs mainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: And did you do any similar location analysis attempting to verify where the Serbs went to where they in fact popped up maybe on the other side of the line?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: In this report in Visegrad report I have analysed all ethnic groups including Serbs. So you have categories in the report in every table.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: On the Serbs, on the Serb population. It is not that this is an unfair analysis. I treat all ethnic groups exactly the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: Thank you, ma'am, no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Good morning, madam. My name is Djuro Cepic. I must admit I envy you because you're going on holiday on Friday.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Excuse me one second. Can I have my transcript back?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] May I?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I have understood your work so far, for the needs of the Prosecution you analysed the changes in the ethnic make-up, and you've already done so in Krajisnik, Plavsic for 37 municipalities, in the Milosevic case for 47 municipalities?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Samac, Odzaci, two municipalities, and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I would like to dwell only on the reports on the changes in the ethnic make-up, and you will agree with me that there have been at least ten.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly the number, but there were many, you are right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And you will agree with me that all these expert reports dealt with different cases and different time periods in the indictment so that the changes in the make-up of the population were researched for different time periods. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, the indictment covered different territories and different time frames, indeed. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You will agree with me that all these analyses of the ethnic make-up, regardless of the case in question, refer to the period from 1991 to 1997 or 1998.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the analysis concerning the changes in the ethnic make-up was something you always did based on two sources of information, the census of 1991 and the voting lists.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the years.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: That's what it says in the report. I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: 1997, 8. I think this is what you meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, the voting list from 1997 and 1998, yes.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: So the question was about the sources, census and the voters 1997 --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do these two sources make it possible for you to observe when radical changes in ethnic make-up occurred? For example, whether it was between 1991 and 1992 or between 1993 and 1994?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did I understand correctly based on the information in the census from 1991 and the voting lists of 1997 and 1998 that these reports are supposed to show what happened in a period covering seven or eight years, but it is not possible to say precisely what happened between 1991 and 1992, or for example, between 1996 and 1997?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, these analyses we presented in all these reports indeed compare only two moments of time, and this is not like a trend analysis or analysis of what causes resulted in the change. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'll ask you as a demographic expert to explain whether the census of 1991 and the voting lists of 1997 and 1998 are compatible sources as far as methodology is concerned.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, it is a simple question, because voters registers is just a sample of trends of data. So as it comes to the methodology of the census I have no doubts this is the best data we can have, the most complete survey covering the entire population made by statistical authority, by professionals with a well-designed questionnaire. Many work around it before the census, like a trial census, and after the census, a post census, a control census, a lot of data, cleansing and so on and so forth. And voters is just part of the census. The voters lists were made by taking the census records. There was no other census in Bosnia, so there was no other way of deciding who is eligible to vote. So the eligible voters had to be included in the census records in order to register to vote or to prove in another way by ID card or residence permit or whatever else that they were eligible to vote. For instance, newcomers from other regions of the former Yugoslavia would have to prove additional because they were not on the census records for Bosnia for '91. So when it comes to the methodology of the voters there is not much I can say. It is just excellent data, simply speaking, because it comes from the census. Excellent in the sense that I don't have to worry about the coverage. I know exactly what's the coverage. It's all registered voters, a big number, and I have all the basic information I need for my work in there included. Of course the deficiencies are there as well as they are in the census, but as long as we understand deficiencies and know how to deal with deficiencies we have a very good chance that we would avoid mistakes and mislead the audience by producing wrong statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So we agree that as far as methodology goes these two sources are not compatible?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Oh, they are compatible. Why they are not compatible? That it wasn't -- voters register is not a survey but it does not mean the sources are compatible. On the contrary, they are very compatible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Cepic, you didn't do statistics in college, evidently.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALARID
utterances.text: One semester, Your Honour, just one semester.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam, would you tell me whether there is any published paper done outside the OTP which used as its source for an analysis of ethnic make-up or migrations voters registers?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, for Bosnia I wouldn't know, really, not that I published. I know for sure I didn't, but I -- I cannot say what others have used for -- for that, the composition. For instance, I am aware of a source which comes from the work of Hans Koschnik for instance in Mostar. He presented his own statistics on the post-conflict population from his own sources by ethnicity. I wouldn't know exactly what he used as a source. Perhaps just municipal records to which he had access. I wouldn't know exactly. But not that I explicitly have seen voters registers published -- well, the ethnic make-up based on voters registration. And by the way, Koschnik's data are very consistent with the results we obtained from the voters lists, you know. You can check on the internet. I can give you the web address for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you. [Interpretation] So we can agree that you have no knowledge of any scholarly paper outside the OTP which uses voters registers as a source for the assessment of ethnic make-up or migrations?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, not based on the voters registers. There were -- there are other things available of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, thank you. [Interpretation] And let's agree about the census. It's been 13 years from the Dayton Accords and peace in Bosnia and there is still no new census. Isn't that a bit odd?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, it's a pity for -- to see this, for me as a demographer, because the census is an invaluable source of information about the population, but I believe there have been very good reasons that there was no census. I wouldn't know exactly what reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The voters registers from 1997 and 1998 that you used as a source of data, do they contain information on ethnic make-up?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, they don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you. [Interpretation] As there is no original data for '97 and '98, that would mean then that you in a way had to produce it by taking it over from other sources. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct. This is what we did using the matching procedure. We matched the records of the voters registers with the census records. It wasn't very difficult because, as I said, the voters register is a part of census data. So linking the two or matching, whatever term you use it's correct, is not very complicated, and in this case a majority of records, at least 2 million, as a matter of fact, or more can be matched immediately using one numeric character, that is JMBG, which is in both, in the voters, in the census, so transferring information between the two is really very, very easy because matching is not a big --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. [In English] Thank you, thank you. [Interpretation] So the census is the only source from which you could derive the ethnic make-up which you say reflects the actual situation in 1997, 1998?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes. It is the only source and the only source that I wanted to use. I didn't want to use reporting ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, [In English] thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: From any other source because perceptions of ethnicity change over time as we know and depend on political situation, economic situation, all kinds of social processes. And in order to produce an unbiased analysis you really have to eliminate the bias of reporting of ethnicity and this is why the census ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] Okay. Thank you. [Interpretation] Can we agree that you in fact are comparing information from 1991 on ethnicity which other information from the same year on ethnicity, and that's only for those voters for whom you were able to take over the ethnic make-up from the census?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: I am not sure that I understand the question, but I guess your question is about ethnicity of voters. If you can confirm?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Ethnicity of voters, the matched records can be taken from the census, and this is what we do; right? Having matched the sources, we can assign ethnicity to every voter record, their ethnicity that was reported in the census records. That means unbiased, unchanged, initial ethnicity. People identified themselves at the outbreak of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And that was a considerably smaller number of inhabitants, right, for whom you managed to take over their ethnicity from the census; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, it is all in the report and in the PowerPoint presentation. I disagree this was a small number, because the number of matched records for the Visegrad municipality, out of 17.800, approximately, we achieved to match 10.850 records in the voters register.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. [In English] We have that in report. We already have that in report.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: It's in the report so I disagree these are small numbers of matched people.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Any number on ethnicity is a good number coming from a big sample.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. [Interpretation] Very well. Now that we're dealing with this topic, can you assess the degree of reliability of the information on ethnic make-up which you present for the year 1997?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: I think it's very reliable. I am speaking of percentages. As I mentioned earlier the absolute size of the population cannot be concluded from the sample size. Sample is just a sample.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: And we don't know the overall total in the post-conflict period, but the percentages, that is the ethnic make-up, ethnic composition, are excellent statistical measures that can be reliably used as for the ethnic composition. So the 19 --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you tell me what the percentage is?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, it's all in the report. We can look at table 3A or page 16 in the PowerPoint presentation. So the percentage of the Serb population dropped -- sorry, increased from about 32.62 to 95 --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] We have it in the report. We have it in the report. Thank you. Thank you. But what I'd like to know now is the difference of 40 per cent of the population seems to be missing from the report. So my question is how can something be correct if 40 per cent is missing?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: So you refer to the unmatched records, aren't you? What is the 40 per cent?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: 40 per cent of the population is missing, madam.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: In my view, nothing is missing from the population. I am explicit about that for '91 we have a complete data that comes from the census, and when it comes to eligible voters it is 17.883, and when it comes to the post-conflict period voters registers we work with a sample, a sample which is a big-size sample, an unbiased sample because there is no underregistration of any ethnic group. So we have a sample of 9.241, which is probably about 60 per cent. As you notice 40 are not there, but a 60 per cent sample in statistics, believe me, it's a very, very good sample. When we work with samples we don't work with these size of samples because it's simply too expensive and nobody has the resources to produce these size of samples.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you. [Interpretation] Well, the next thing I'd like to know is the following: As you are representing the ethnic make-up only for the population which is of age, could you tell us what percentage of minors you have excluded from your observations? What is the percentage?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, it is all in the report as well, and if you refer to the slide 15 from the PowerPoint presentation. So the excluded persons who were not eligible to vote is 3.316, which is 15.6 per cent of the 1991 population.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And we can only guess in the meantime what the birth rate was, because we have no clear data on that; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, we didn't look at the birth rate, so why would I be interested right now at the birth -- in the birth rate?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Well, because newborn babies are also citizens, they're also part of the population; right? If someone was born in 1992 or 1993, that person is now 15.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: No, sir. You're trying to say the new birth could significantly change the ethnic makeup in the post-conflict period. I don't think so. I don't think so. This kind of big sample as a voters register is really very close to the overall statistics in the entire population. I will give you an example from the report --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. I have heard your reply. Thank you. We do have the report and I have studied it in great detail. You will agree that in your analysis the percentage of 15.6, with which is not small.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: It's not small but it doesn't have a significant impact, if any, on the ethnic composition obtained from the voters register.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: That's the beauty of the sample, sir, that we don't really have to have all the individuals in the sample in order to produce good statistics, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Could you tell us to what extent those who have been excluded from the register influence the validity of your results for 1997?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: I already answered. They don't significantly impact on the results I obtained from my sample, not at all. Look, sir, we can refer to the sample from the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, thank you, thank you. You have answered for me. Thank you and we have report, thank you, Doctor. [Interpretation] Madam, all the voters in 1997, were you able to verify that they actually existed in the census?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, if -- they come from the census so they existed in the census. It is not data that was made up by anybody. It was taken -- the voters register comes from the census. So the matching rate for the voters as the entire data set is about 80 per cent. So 80 per cent were matched directly with the census. In my view, knowing that there are deficiencies in the census data, spelling mistakes and some incompleteness of important items, if you achieve a matching rate of 80 per cent, it is a very high matching rate. So there is no doubt that the voters are, a vast majority of them, in the census, because it has been proven through the matching.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: So it's not a hundred per cent. You've just told us it's 80 per cent, one-fifth, that is. Does it mean that you're excluding a certain number of people from the voters registers?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The 20 per cent unmatched records are excluded.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I'll ask you a question as a statistician. In statistics, can one tolerate poor coverage of the population or is that to be considered an error?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: What do you mean by poor coverage of the population?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Well, I understand that your basic professional education is as a statistician, so I'm asking you is poor coverage of the population in statistics tolerated or is it considered an error?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: But you are very vague in your question. In order to be able to answer the question I need to understand what a poor coverage is. I don't really know, because in my study here, census is definitely not the case of poor coverage of the population. Neither are the voters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: How much is covered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Census, it is basically the entire population, and the voters is all -- very considerable part of the population. Well, how much per cent it is? Let me think. Yeah, about 80 per cent or something, if I'm not wrong. So it is again not a poor coverage. So poor coverage, if -- if -- well, we sometimes work with small samples of 1.000 or 2.000 individuals who at present --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I rather expect that's what Mr. Cepic has in mine. Are you talking about the samples, Mr. Cepic?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have a difference of 20 per cent. Those are people who have not been matched, and I'm interested in that difference of 20 per cent. In statistics can it be tolerated or is it an error, because it amounts to one-fifth of the population which has not been matched, as the doctor has just confirmed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Let me just ask the doctor to comment on that now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And then Judge David has a question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, as I'm trying to explain, we work with a sample from the voters register. That the 20 per cent are unmatched and excluded doesn't mean that the remaining records constitute a poor coverage sample, not at all. Not at all. There are no rules in statistics how much of the population must be covered in order to work with a good sample. If a sample is representative, even a small sample of a few hundreds or thousands individuals will be considered a good sample. It is a matter of how representative the sample is of the entire population. And I am 100 per cent convinced in this case. There is no doubt here about the poor -- the good coverage of the sample.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I think that Honourable Judge David.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: I would like to ask you two questions and these two questions are not in order to show you my poor knowledge of inferential statistics. As you know, you have mentioned always as a proof and reliability and confidence of your conclusions chi-square.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Which is a measure of discrepancy and to my poor knowledge that measure of discrepancy exclude the possibility of the new hypothesis which is to say an association by chance. So you are giving us in chi-square a high degree of discrepancy which is to say a high degree of probability that these inferences are unrelated to resolve by chance.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, these results I put in the report are all shown not to be resulting from chance. They are shown that the probability of error is extremely low. It is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Second question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: -- insignificant. This is very good question, Your Honour, I must admit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Second question. Can you be -- this is a part of inferential statistics, isn't that correct? The chi-square is a measure of deviation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, excellent, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: It's a measure of deviation. Could you say it's part of inferential statistics, which is to say that based on these values, you could obtain what is called empirical generalisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Okay. Empirical generalisations are not a predictor in the sense of a priori adoptions but you could obtain reliability and confidence playing from the viewpoint of a statistical data. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: That's all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Cepic, apparently you needed to have Judge David as your teacher.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: But we could go on like this for hours, you know, but I hope you're bringing this to an end now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'll try to be fast and to use --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are not in a university seminar.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Doctor, is my understanding correct, you compare the census results and the voters register. On the one hand you have information on a part of the population constituted by adults and then on the other hand you have the underage sections of the population comprising maybe 50 per cent, maybe 60 per cent or up to 70 per cent. Methodologically speaking, can you compare these two kinds of information from two different sources that actually studied different sectors of the population?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: I think you are wrong by saying that when I use the census data I compare all ages with the voters being above 18 in 1997, '8. No. If you look at the report then you see that I only work using the census data with those born before 1980. This is those who later will become -- would become eligible to vote in 1997, '8 elections so I am working with the same type of information, exactly the same type of information in both cases. When it comes to age distribution, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I think I actually asked you something else. What about the methodology? Is this comparable, the two sources that comprise different sectors of the population, methodologically?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, sir, I think you -- you misread any report perhaps. Well, I work with cohort data, that means these are individual data. I'm following a group of individuals reported in the census all these individuals I require to be born before 1980. I have the individual data. I can do that. I can restrict the data. And I trace them in the voters register. So these are exactly the same people we are talking about. They come initially from the census. I look for them in the voters. I find them in the voters, I take them and I compare so there is nothing in the methodology you can criticise. It is a perfect way of doing things, thanks to the fact that I have individual-level sources like the census and the voters.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: As an expert, what would be a tolerable statistical aberration [Realtime transcript read in error "statistic collaboration"] in serious research or for the purposes of serious research?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Collaboration.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Statistical aberration.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Aberration, sorry, aberration. Well, collaboration is in the transcript. This is why. Well, commonly accepted level of error in inferential statistics is about -- is 5 per cent, say. So that would satisfy your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Statistical error, 5 per cent, yes indeed, that's true. And what was the percentage of error in the way names were written in the census and what was the percentage in voters registers?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, I'm -- I am afraid that this question doesn't make sense at all. I wouldn't be able to give you an assessment of the error level in the spelling of names, and this is not inferential statistics of course so we are not using any test or anything right now. I have no answer to this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: You have no answer?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: If I may add --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, please let her add what she wishes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think this 5 per cent level, it is just a commonly I said accepted, but there are no strict rules in statistics that 5 per cent is accepted but 5.1 is not accepted. It -- well, error level is an indication of the quality of the find -- of the result. So I think sticking to these kinds of rules I -- I don't like it simply, you know. So I could give you an assessment of the errors in the spelling names by, for instance, presenting you with samples of names as originally reported in the census and then later as we corrected them. This can be done and then you can think of the error level, but the thing is that the corrections that we made in the names were very thorough based on three separate procedures which resulted in a great improvement. We see this great improvement when comparing the census data with other sources in cross-referencing with other sources in which the numeric JMBG, the ID, personal ID is unavailable and names have to be used in matching. So there is a great degree of consistency in our corrected names with names reported in other sources and we have a lot of other sources and good sources as well. For instance, for mortality we have two great databases established by professional statisticians from both RS and federal statistical institutes, and the names in these sources they are huge databases, all together 140.000 death records and there is a great overlap of the names.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: So this tells you that the corrections were very good actually, although I cannot assign an error level right now, but I can give you in a descriptive way my assessment of the -- of the corrections and of the improvement.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you have complete records on this?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: What do you mean by complete records? Statistics you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The errors while you were working and getting this confirmed. Did you keep any sort of records on this?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: A quantitative error measure you mean, do I have that I can give you for the corrections in the names? This is what you meant?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Errors, individual errors that you spotted in relation to Visegrad municipality. Did you keep track of those? Did you keep any records?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, we keep track of the corrections. Most definitely we do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: With all the names?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: From Visegrad and other municipalities, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Can we see that, please? Can that be handed over to us completely?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: I believe it is part of the census data. You can see it most certainly. At our premises in the OTP we will disclose this part of the census data for your study. I cannot give you a hard copy because it's impossible. But you can certainly have access to it and study it without any problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I need your records on that, on these errors. That's what I need, on an individual basis. Do you have that or not?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we understand each other, but in my view you are requesting me -- from me two lists, names as originally reported in the census and corrected names. Is this what you want?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam, I'm looking for records on these errors that were noticed. You did some work. You cross-referenced the names from the voters register to those in the census. I suppose you kept records on the side. I need records on every name in Visegrad. That's what I need now. Do you have that or do you not?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, I just answered that I do have it and you can have it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: For each name.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: For each name. Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Just a minute. Just a minute. Ms. Marcus, why have you brought this evidence? It's a simple question. I think we believe we all know the answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Thank you for the question. The evidence was brought as a contextual background to the case, to put the crimes that have been charged in the contextual setting of the pattern, of the overall pattern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does it go to the proof of any --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the President, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Does it go to the proof of any of the -- of any of the charges?

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we would say it goes to the proof of the common elements of the crimes charged, widespread, systematic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. So it does go beyond mere background.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Yes. In that respect, Your Honours, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cepic. I think you should be coming to an end now.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm trying to do my best, Your Honour. I'm trying, but this witness is expert, and I -- I really compressed all my questions to make it short and to have the shortest Defence case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: All right. Proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, about these records. Did you enter corrections in relation to names as contained in the original records, the census and so on and so forth?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, as I said, I have both, the original names and the corrected names. So the corrections are there. But without the original items to be changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: And this will all be made available to us for a look; right?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, here at the OTP. Yes, you can have access to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. All right. Now -- now, I want to know about this source --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: The third source, the ICRC lists, something you mention. This is from 1998.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: No. The ICRC list used in the updated report is from 2005.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm. And that list contains numerous errors. There are numerous discrepancies between the list that you showed us yesterday and the ICRC list; right? Because I actually cross-referenced the names in the two lists, and my assistant helped me with that and we realised there were numerous discrepancies. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, there are some deficiencies in the ICRC list, but I don't think I agree fully with you that the -- there are -- there is a high degree of inconsistencies between the ICRC list and other sources. I wouldn't agree. There are inconsistencies. As I said on Monday, there are errors in the date of birth or date of disappearance. Yes, there are errors, but this is not -- I wouldn't see it as a large-scale errors.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Sir -- or madam, Mr. Domazet asked you in the Vasiljevic trial that only 20 something persons went missing on the 14th of June according to the ICRC list. However, according to the indictment that figure, at least according to what the OTP are trying to tell us is quite higher. You will agree with me that this is a striking discrepancy.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: It depends how you see the ICRC list. If you expect that the ICRC list is a complete source as the census is, then I would say this discrepancy is striking, but the ICRC nobody claimed is a complete information about victims from any area in Bosnia. This list is a very special source, very different from sources reporting on known deaths. ICRC list only reports on missing persons of whom we don't know what happened to these individuals. The families reported them missing at some point. So this is --

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: This explains the discrepancy. We are speaking in the indictment of both, known deaths and missing persons, and ICRC only reports on the missing persons. There is no way these two sources would give you the exact same overall total of victims on a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. And you will agree with me no doubt that when we look at the ICRC information, the only thing that's recorded is the last time a person was seen by whoever reports this missing person. Is that right? This is information about when someone was last seen somewhere at a certain point in time.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, this is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the two 0s, if you look at those lists, that means we don't know the exact date or month when a person was last seen. Is that not what it means?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: In the reported dates, yes. The code two 0s means no date, no month.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Therefore, we may now conclude that the records are actually records of when persons were last seen, the ICRC means, I mean.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, this is what -- what we agreed on. These are records on persons who were last seen at some point.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: In your analysis did you compare the list of missing persons or when persons were last seen with the list of members of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Of what army?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: BH army.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] BH army, yes.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: At some point we did, especially recently for the use in the Popovic case, we made such a comparison, we cross-referenced the ICRC list with the military records of the BH army, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: But that wasn't done in the Visegrad trial because this is not reflected in the report, is it?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, it wasn't done, and it can be done if you wish to see this cross-referencing. I don't see any problem. Such a result can be easily produced if you wish to see it. But I want to add that military records is not a proof that the person died in combat situation. It is just a membership in the army or in an institution related to the army like for instance the Minister of Defence or a person who would work in the production sector providing goods or services to army and died in the conflict would be reported as well. So I don't think it is -- it depends on what you want to do. It is just an indication like a monitoring of the status of victims reported by other sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps request information in order to ascertain whether maybe some of the missing persons had taken part in combat, in armed action and perhaps perished as a result?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't request any information from anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'll try to put you questions as fast as I can. [Interpretation] Something about your methodology. Is this the kind of methodology that is used for purposes of scientific research?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Well, yes, most certainly it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In each of your reports you use the matching method. Is this a method that is normally used by demographers?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: I think it is. It's used overall. If you do a Google search, you are talking about nothing else but matching. There is a big literature body related to matching. Matching resulted from the field of IT information technology studies and developed very rapidly in recent years, so there is a great number of publications. If you want I can give you a list.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: This method, Doctor, please, I'm trying to get through this as quickly as possible. Is this method something that is used by demographers generally speaking, yes or no, please, if you can?

utterances.speaker: EWA TABEAU [Recalled]
utterances.text: Yes, especially in historical demography.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Meaning this method is -- [In English] I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, is there a possibility to construct through inference some empirical generalisations from your data and, without asking you to venture now, do you conceive the possibility of establishing some generalisations or to verbalise these interrelations that you have shown in your study in a sort of inferential systematic way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I see it possible, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Could you give me an example so everybody will grasp what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Well, for instance confidence intervals [Realtime transcript omitted "intervals"] can be associated with the estimated ethnic composition. This is the first example I can easy think of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We didn't get that. What is it that can be associated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Confidence intervals can be associated with the estimated ethnic composition based on the voters data. So this would be a formal error measurement that can be offered in order to tell the reliability statistically speaking of these results. When it comes to matching, there can be formal measures of error associated with the matching results as well, and this can be presented in a formal way as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, may I continue, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I'm still trying to see whether I understood confidence intervals.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This is a statistical concept showing as a matter of fact more than just the point estimate that is now presented in the report. In table 3A as far as I remember I am showing ethnic composition as percentages, and these are actually like point estimates. Just one single number for every ethnic group. But as a matter of fact, because I've been working with a sample, this is just one of possible values for this per cent. There might be a range of values associated with the point estimate, and this range can be required to contain values that are highly probable. Let me say 95 per cent confidence interval would show us the values that are -- were produced with 95 per cent of confidence, so at the 5 per cent error level. And I can assure you we have done something exercise of this kind that confidence intervals associated with these kind of measures of ethnic composition will be very narrow because of the big sample size.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: A second point, Dr. Tabeau. As to the interrelations of the variables of ethnicity that you have in location that you have detected, could also be that they could be -- we could generalise and establish interrelations, you know, in a sort of axiomatic mode.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not sure I understand the question fully.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DAVID
utterances.text: The -- from empirical generalisations could we construct an orderly system of inferences around the interrelation of variables that you have shown in the study?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, I think I understand what my brother is saying, because I don't think you answered his question. I believe his question was whether from all the data that you have garnered you're able to -- to make some generalisations. So the confidential interval is not a generalisation. He's asking whether you can make some inferential generalisation on the basis of the data that you have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I -- I'm not sure that I understand, but I believe that certain general conclusions I try to put forward in this report, and I didn't associate any error level for these general observations, but I think that general conclusions based on results obtained in a statistically responsible manner most certainly can be seen as reliable. So I concentrated in this report on presenting the statistics as reliable because they are reliable. This is good statistical material, and when drawing general conclusions I didn't actually repeat the fact that they are solid statistical conclusions but they are. They are. Any general observation of the kind, for instance, as I am saying that these dramatic change in the ethnic composition could not result from normal demographic or socioeconomic factors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I see. So you have in fact --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do have in this report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: -- made conclusions, drawn conclusions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And they are summarised in the report and presentations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So they are all based on solid statistical material which can be formally associated with error levels and therefore the conclusions can be taken as responsible and statistically reliable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In fact, the purpose of Mr. Cepic's cross-examination is to challenge the validity of those conclusions, because to the extent that he succeeds in challenging them, then he -- he plants a dent in that part of the Prosecution's case that relies on -- on your data as evidence of, say, widespread and systematic crimes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Judge --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: I, too, have a question, Dr. Tabeau, just to be clear about your conclusion at the end of your PowerPoint. Maybe it is in your report, but what I would like to know is in terms of the numbers in the Visegrad region for the month of -- month of May and June, 1992, how many persons went missing, how many disappeared, and how many died. Do we have -- I'm sure it's somewhere in your report, but can you, just to guide me through your report give me those precise numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: How many went missing, how many disappeared, and now deceased.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, actually the term disappeared and missing are used as synonyms so it is both the same category. This is just a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Because you say 62 per cent of missing all missing disappeared so ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Of all missing in '92, these appeared during these two months.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Right, I see.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So this is another [overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Well, if I can -- in relation to this conclusion, if we can perhaps can use slide 25 of the PowerPoint presentation.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I have it for the ELMO if you'd like. Sorry, I have it for the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So slide 25. I show in this table, which is in the report, the distribution of going missing by month of disappearance starting with April 1992 until December 1992. It is just the year 1992. All ten municipalities in the Visegrad region are included. We are looking at the Visegrad, which is of course the main point of interest, and starting from May and then continuing in June and in July the numbers are extraordinary high. So -- and this is actually typical of the region, so that means in other municipalities we see the same pattern, and when only the two numbers for May and June of the missing persons are taken into account, all together these two months account for about 62 per cent of all missing in 1992. This is a very big number knowing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VAN DEN WYNGAERT
utterances.text: Do we know how many people deceased? Do we know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, we don't know this. I can't answer straight away. It would be necessary to put pieces of information together. We have victim lists from the indictment. We have additional victims. We have missing persons. All these put together would result in overall numbers of victims. I would have to do that, but it can be done. But the number of missing in '92, the entire year '92 as shown on slide 22 is 2.528, which is a big number, which is a very big number, yes. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cepic -- well, we are now a minute beyond the time for the break, so we'll adjourn.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cepic.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Dr. Tabeau, I'll try to make the specific questions, and if you are able to give me short and precise answers just to pass this as fast as we can. Thank you. [Interpretation] Madam, looking at these tables, let's have a look at table number 9. It's on the screen, so let's look at it briefly, because I'm intrigued by something I noticed in this data. [In English] Could we have on the screen page -- the previous page, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: If you tell us which page I'll be happy to give you the page for the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: 21st page in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: Is this on the report or the PowerPoint?

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: From report.

utterances.speaker: MS. MARCUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. That's Exhibit P118 marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: Madam, while we're waiting for it to come up, Mr. Helge Brunborg and you on the -- you drew up a report on Srebrenica, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter missed the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We actually wrote several reports together on Srebrenica with Helge Brunborg, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. CEPIC
